Neiman told the DCNF that Barlow, who defeated Degenfelder, proved he was not a conservative through his voting record, particularly on issues pertaining to energy and abortion.

“Eric Barlow is not a conservative,” Neiman told the DCNF. “His voting record does not show that … He’s the establishment candidate, that’s just the facts. [There’s] video of him testifying before Congress in the opposition to our legacy industries, coal and gas. I don’t know how you can be conservative and be fighting against the very things that give us national security, and to be portraying yourself as a conservative in that respect, I think, is impossible with that kind of a record.”

Evidence Based Wyoming’s Doug Gerard wrote that Barlow was affiliated with the anti-coal, anti-oil and anti-gas Powder River Basin Resource Council. In 2013, Barlow reportedly voted with a majority of Democrats 90% of the time and was the sixth most liberal Republican in the House.

Barlow voted to raise taxes on the oil and gas industry, sponsored an amendment in 2014 to accept Obamacare funding in Wyoming and voted to change the definition of marriage, according to Gerard’s report.

“Eric Barlow’s campaign presents him as a mainstream conservative Republican. His legislative record tells a more complex story,” Gerard wrote in the report. “He is a substantive legislator with deep expertise in healthcare, genuine engagement with energy policy, and credible Second Amendment credentials. However, his overall voting pattern—particularly his fiscal scores, composite political rankings, and extraordinary defection record—places him firmly in the liberal wing of the Wyoming Republican Party.”

Barlow’s campaign did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment.

Barlow voted against a bill to ban abortion after a heartbeat was detected, according to the report. However, he voted for bills that restricted abortions.

“Eric’s record on life in particular, pro-life legislation, is long,” the spokesperson said. “So I don’t think that a donation reflects anything about his policy. It more reflects his leadership style. Which is a respectful leadership style.”

The gubernatorial candidate made property tax reduction a major centerpiece of his campaign. Gerard’s report cited three instances where Barlow voted against property tax relief when the legislation did not pass by large margins. He voted against a bill in 2019 that would have given seniors property tax exemptions.

Barlow received over $1.7 million in total contributions, according to Transparency USA. He received over $168,000 in direct donations from the Civil Leadership PAC, $40,000 from Conpac Contractors, $5,000 from the Credit Union PAC, $5,000 from the Lawyers Active in Wyoming PAC and $1,000 from the Union Pacific Corporation Fund for Effective Government, according to Transparency USA.

Wyoming’s Turn PAC, a federal PAC aligned with Republican Wyoming Rep. Harriet Hageman’s Senate campaign, poured about $1.45 million into opposing Barlow and supporting Degenfelder, Cowboy State Daily reported. Hageman won her Senate primary in August.

Trump won Wyoming 72.3% to 26.1% against former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. In 2022, former Republican Rep. Liz Cheney lost her primary reelection bid to Hageman by a 30-point margin after sitting on the Jan. 6 Select Committee and voting to impeach Trump in January 2021. She campaigned for Democrats, such as Harris.

news.title: MEME-FODDER MARK: Carney blew up the trade deal. Now Canada is the punch line.
news.text:
After Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared that Canada was “at war” with the United States and walked away from a proposed trade deal last month, Canada quickly became an object of ridicule in Washington.

But after blowing up the trade deal, Carney has been less eager to explain exactly what happened. He has ignored Official Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre’s demand to reconvene Parliament or provide the Conservative leader with details of the failed trade negotiations.

'How are we going to be at war with Canada? What, are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton Mall and sic them on us?'

Carney has offered a broad explanation for walking away, arguing that Washington was demanding concessions that threatened Canadian sovereignty and could eventually wipe out important Canadian industries, particularly auto manufacturing.

American officials tell a very different story.

'Best deal available'

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer flatly denied Carney’s allegations that President Donald Trump wanted somehow to interfere with Quebec culture or erode official bilingualism in Canada.

“We had agreed to, as I've shared before in the press, really the best deal available to any country on the planet with respect to Canada,” Greer told CBC News in the aftermath of Carney's withdrawal.

What Carney did emerge to address Tuesday was something else: the memes.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he told reporters Tuesday.

As with all attempts to demand that people on the internet stop making fun of you, Carney’s statement had the opposite effect. Even American officials couldn’t resist a little trolling.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent mocked Carney’s claim that the countries were “at war.”

“I think this is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match,” Bessent said. 

“I mean, we're not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? What, are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton Mall and sic them on us?”

Looking out for number one?

Then Bessent got more serious.

“He came to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump agenda. He was 20 points behind in the polls, and then he started this. 

"It's unfortunate that he's not doing what's best for the Canadian people. He's doing what is best for the Liberal Party, what's best for Mark Carney, and in the long run, the Canadian people are going to see through that.”

Bessent reiterated the administration’s contention that Canada had been offered “the best trade deal of any country on the globe” before Carney walked away from it at "the last minute.”

Carney may not have been the only Canadian politician responsible for blowing up the agreement.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford reportedly pushed for better treatment of Ontario's auto industry and resisted returning American alcohol to the shelves of Ontario's government-owned liquor stores.

Since the deal collapsed, Ford has even suggested that Alberta could cut off oil shipments to the United States — an idea he has floated before.

There was an awkward problem with Ford’s threat: Ontario itself depends on Alberta oil that travels through the United States. Enbridge’s Line 5 crosses Michigan before returning to Canada and supplying Ontario refineries.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith quickly rejected Ford’s idea, warning that cutting off Alberta energy exports to the United States would be “extremely harmful to Canadians.”

RELATED: MILK MONEY: How Mark Carney chose the dairy cartel — and China — over a Trump trade deal

 Bloomberg/Kirsty O'Conner/Nuria Gonzalez-Sanchez/Getty Images

Key role for American Democrat

There are also legitimate questions about other sticking points in the failed negotiations. Carney remains committed to Canada's heavily protected dairy sector, opposed to reviving the Keystone XL pipeline, and increasingly interested in expanding trade with China. The Trump administration has also accused Canada of serving as a route for Chinese steel transshipped into the United States to evade American trade restrictions.

And the questions about Carney’s handling of the United States don’t end with the trade deal.

Take Maia Johnson, the American and registered Democrat with ties to the Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris campaigns, whom Carney promoted to the newly created position of chief operating officer in the prime minister’s office. Before the promotion, Johnson held the revealing title of “senior adviser, United States stakeholder strategy” — meaning Carney had already put an American Democratic operative in a key role advising him on how to deal with the United States.

'Manufactured' crisis

Whatever was going on inside Carney’s office, the Trump administration has been remarkably consistent about what happened to the deal.

“Canada was going to have the best trade deal in the world,” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters. “And what happened was that Canada walked away. We had a deal. We shook hands. The president announced it, right? Everybody was positive. Canada made the decision for political purposes. They wanted to walk away.”

Lutnick also rejected Carney's contention that Washington had sought concessions involving Quebec and the French language.

“Do I care about how the Quebecois speak?” Lutnick said. “I mean, what could matter less to America? We don't care.”

“This is manufacturing,” he continued. “That's why the president put out a Truth [Social post] saying it was a complete lie.”

news.title: Top Trump officials 'left holding the bag' as GOP braces for 'fallout'
news.text:
According to one poll after another, soaring prices are a top concern of voters in the 2026 midterms. President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and inflation, polls show, is a key factor. That includes grocery prices, and according to Bloomberg News columnist Mary Ellen Klas, the "political fallout" has repercussions not only for Trump, but for Republicans in general — including top Trump administration officials like Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"Trump may not care about the political fallout, but his likely successors — Vance, Secretary Marco Rubio and every Republican left in Congress — should," Klas argues in her Bloomberg column. "They're the ones who will be left holding the (grocery) bag."

Vance and Rubio are both being mentioned as possible GOP presidential candidates for 2028.

Klas, in her column, emphasizes that "food prices play an outsized role in how Americans view affordability."

"When you're bombarded with bigger price tags and shrinking product sizes on every trip to the grocery store," Klas writes, "it's an in-your-face reminder that we're losing purchasing power. It's leading to widespread anxiety. According to an Associated Press-NORC poll released in August, 41 percent of Americans say they are concerned about being able to afford groceries, up from 24 percent in April." 

Rising prices, according to polls, played a major role in the outcome of the 2024 presidential election. Trump relentlessly attacked the Democratic nominee, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, on inflation, promising to lower prices "on Day 1" if he won. But roughly 19 and one half months into Trump's second presidency, inflation is still a major worry for voters.

"If the 2024 election turned on the price of eggs," Klas explains, "the 2026 midterm may well turn on the price of the rest of what's in Americans' shopping carts. And 2028 could shape up the same way: According to forecasts, eating is going to get more expensive for at least another year. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service predicts that the average food bill will climb at least 3 percent in 2026 and another 2.4 percent in 2027."

The Bloomberg News columnist adds, "Those averages don't account for the commodities that will see even sharper price increases this year. Among them, beef will be up 9.8 percent and fresh vegetables up 5.9 percent. Perhaps the hardest thing for voters to get used to is the cumulative rise in the cost of groceries. The USDA (United States Department of Agriculture) says overall food prices have increased only 3 percent in the last year, but since January 2020, they've risen 30 percent."

Michigan State University economist David Ortega warns that food prices "rarely come down." 

Ortega, in an interview, told Klas, "Since the turn of the last century, food prices have decreased only twice — and they were both for a very short period of time. So, when voters and consumers hear from politicians, 'We're going to bring prices down,' it sets the expectation that it's possible when reality and economics point the other direction."

news.title: Mid-Day Digest — September 4, 2026
news.text:
“Dangerous” is the keyword in today’s Washington Post headline about the labor force under President Donald Trump. Stuart Anderson and Mark Regets, both of the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), authored an op-ed to dissect some numbers on immigration and the job market ahead of Labor Day, and they issue a stern warning to the president.

Donald Trump is on track to become the first president in a century to oversee a U.S. labor force that will be smaller when he leaves office than when he entered. Since the start of his second term, the number of people in the United States who are either employed or looking for a job has dropped by 1.6 million — and it’s largely because of Trump’s immigration restrictions. Unless those policies change, a shrinking workforce will cause slower economic growth and lead to more expensive public debt.

Anderson and Regets aren’t left-wingers. Anderson formerly worked for the libertarian Cato Institute and served under President George W. Bush as policy director at the Immigration and Naturalization Service. Both are pro-immigration and anti-illegal immigration — a long-standing Republican stance.

But let’s back up a minute.

President Joe Biden and his inept border czar Kamala Harris allowed at least 10 million illegals to cross the border and stay in the country during their four-year term. The migrant flood created a humanitarian crisis at the border, added to a crime wave Democrats fomented over George Floyd, and triggered an immense backlash among voters disinclined to see our nation overrun by lawlessness. Trump promised that, if reelected, he would cut off the flow and begin deportations.

The NFAP duo notes, “The Bureau of Labor Statistics household survey for July recorded a decline of 1.8 million foreign-born workers since January 2025.” Overall, there are three million fewer immigrants in the U.S. since Trump took office.

Yes, Trump is doing what he promised.

That said, Anderson and Regets are correct that there are trade-offs. Historically, the labor force has grown at a generally steady rate. It suddenly shrinking will have real economic consequences. “Immigrants are not only workers,” they observe, “but also consumers.” Fewer consumers means lower demand, which means slower business growth.

Despite warnings from the likes of Paul Ehrlich about an overpopulation crisis, people are resources, and we need an increasing population. (I try to remind myself of this while sitting in rush hour traffic.)

Still, there are some important caveats. The pair mention demographics only in passing, and only regarding data from 20 years ago: “Falling birth rates slowed the expansion of the U.S.-born labor force after the early 2000s, but thanks to immigration the number of total workers still rose by 1.6 million during Barack Obama’s first term and by 3.9 million during his second.”

Importing labor to cover for Americans not having babies is not a good or permanent solution. But the birth rate has been falling for decades now, with no sign of changing course anytime soon. You can thank any number of factors for that, but it seems the culture has produced more Gloria Steinems and Lindsay Clancy defenders than babies. Until militant feminism recedes and married men and women start producing more children, the demographic spiral will continue.

Another factor is the number of unemployed or underemployed American men. Our Samantha Koch delved into this underreported crisis earlier this week, as did our Weekly Verdict podcast team. Koch said, “Roughly 44 million working-age men are now outside the labor force — about nine million more than in 2012 — while male labor-force participation has fallen to just 66.8%.”

In other words, the size of the labor force is not necessarily an immigration problem. And men leaving the workforce is both the result and the cause of a whole host of other problems, including the demographic spiral.

There is, however, good news on the economic front. The economy created 162,000 jobs in August, the best showing since April. The headline unemployment rate remained at 4.1%.

Next up is a manufacturing boom. Political analyst Gary Bauer sums it up in a bulleted list:

New factory orders rose 0.9% in July, nearly double the “experts’” predictions.Durable-goods orders are up 7.6%.Machinery orders are up 12.3%.Computer and electronics orders are up 14.3%.Primary metals orders are up 14.4%.Industrial machinery and communications equipment orders are up nearly 40%.Manufacturing job openings rose to 580,000 in July, up 35% from one year ago.

There are reasons to dislike President Trump’s tariffs, but it certainly seems that they’re spurring at least some of this growth.

In any case, the most important policies for economic expansion are low taxes, limited regulations, and a secure border with sane immigration numbers. For good measure, let’s throw in growing families.

Happy Labor Day.

news.title: Some Republicans want Trump to stay away from their midterm campaigns: ‘We’ve told them he cannot come’
news.text:
Republicans in some of the most competitive races in the country have told President Donald Trump's political operation that they do not want him campaigning in their districts this fall — including in seats he won by double digits two years ago.

"We've told them he cannot come," a senior Republican working on a competitive House race in such a district told Politico, which reported the account Friday. "Candidly, he would not be helpful here."

The remark appears in a survey of more than two dozen Republican lawmakers, candidates and operatives published by the outlet that found the party has settled on no unified approach to a president whose approval rating has reached the lowest levels ever recorded for him. 

Four Republican operatives involved in the conversations said that battleground Republicans have relayed the message directly to Trump's team, while three others said leading GOP pollsters have advised vulnerable incumbents to limit or avoid mentioning the president on the trail altogether.

Yet it appears Trump has no intention of staying home. At a Rose Garden dinner on Wednesday, he told battleground Republicans he would be heavily involved in the final 30 days of the campaign.

The Republicans’ preemptive rejection of Trump on the campaign trail comes as his polling has reached levels that show him less popular than at any other point in his political career.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll last month put Trump's approval at 33 percent in a survey of 1,167 — the lowest reading of his presidency in that poll's history, and unchanged across three consecutive weeks. On the economy, 71 percent disapproved and 22 percent approved. Nearly half of respondents, 47 percent, named the cost of living as the most important issue of the midterms.

A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll taken August 21-26 had him at 32 percent approval against 64 percent disapproval. Its more consequential finding for Republicans on the ballot was internal to the party: Trump's approval among Republicans has fallen from 89 percent in April 2025 to 75 percent, and among people who voted for him in 2024 it is down 10 points. Just 25 percent said he is handling the war in Iran well, against 68 percent who said he is not.

Quinnipiac recorded an all-time low of 32 percent in late July. AP-NORC had him at 33 percent, eight points below where he stood at the same point in his first term. Pew Research Center found in July that 42 percent of voters described their coming congressional vote as a vote against Trump, against 22 percent who called it a vote for him.

In mid-August, Reuters/Ipsos found that for the first time in roughly a decade, more voters said they trust Democrats to handle the economy than Republicans, 38 percent to 35 percent.

Not every survey agrees. A Harvard CAPS/Harris poll of 2,100 registered voters taken August 28-30 had Trump at 44 percent, up two points from July, with 52 percent disapproving — an outlier against the rest of the recent field. That poll still gave Democrats the advantage on the generic congressional ballot, 51 percent to 49, and by 54 to 46 among independents.

The comparison Republicans running in swing seats are likely to find least comfortable is a historical one. Gallup had Trump's approval at 40 percent during the week of September 3-9, 2018. That November, Republicans lost 41 House seats. He is now polling below that figure in most national surveys, and the Cook Political Report has Democrats favored to retake the chamber.

Trump's super PAC is holding a war chest of more than $400 million that Republican campaigns badly need deployed, according to Politico — money that gives the president leverage over candidates who might otherwise keep their distance, and a reason for them not to say publicly what they are saying privately.

One House Republican in a competitive race described the guidance they had received from pollsters and operatives to Politico in blunter terms: "You're f***ed if you mention him too much, and you're also f***ed if you don't stay in his good graces."

Where Trump says he plans to go is itself a measure of the problem. When he described his campaign schedule on Wednesday, he named Alaska, for Senator Dan Sullivan, and Texas, where he intends to boost Ken Paxton — two states he carried by roughly 14 points in 2024 and where Republican incumbents are nonetheless facing serious Democratic challenges.

Party officials are publicly rejecting the premise. Representative Richard Hudson, who chairs the National Republican Congressional Committee, told Politico that "based on our polling, the President's a net positive in every district," and said he has been encouraging Trump to hold more rallies. 

The Republican National Committee's national press secretary, Natalie Baldassarre, warned that members who keep the president at arm's length "risk alienating their base" and losing 15 to 20 percent of their key Republican voters. The committee renamed its candidate recruitment program from "Young Guns" to the "MAGA Majority" earlier this year, and no candidate joined the list without Trump's endorsement.

Plenty of Republicans do want him. Representative Rob Bresnahan, defending a Pennsylvania seat Trump carried by nearly nine points, said he would welcome a presidential visit — "Sure, absolutely" — while denying that he had seen Trump's approval rating in his own district. Florida Representative Anna Paulina Luna, who attended Wednesday's dinner, said the president was in good spirits and added: "And boy, oh boy, does MAGA Inc. have a war chest."

Others are threading it more carefully. New York Representative Mike Lawler, one of three House Republicans representing a district Kamala Harris won in 2024, is running an advertisement built around Trump calling him "a pain in the a**" at a recent rally. Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, who attended the White House dinner, is skipping next week's Republican midterm convention in Dallas. "I can't control what the president's going to say at the convention," he said, "but I can control where I'm at."

White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales did not address questions about the president's approval ratings or about Republicans asking him not to visit, instead listing his record on taxes, prescription drug costs, the border, crime, energy and stock market returns.

"The choice has never been more clear," she said.

Yet one battleground operative told Politico the whole debate is beside the point, because there is nowhere for Republicans to run.

"Every cycle people try to do that, and it looks disingenuous," the operative said. "At this point, Trump is baked into everything."

news.title: Republicans are the party of the working class | Shaun McCutcheon
news.text:
For generations, the political map of America was simple and stable.

Democrats enjoyed the loyalty of organized labor. Republicans drew their strength from business. Union halls were Democratic strongholds. The Republican Party was associated with corporate boardrooms and country clubs.

That map has been redrawn. Conservatives now speak the language of wage earners, and a growing share of working-class voters are noticing.

The change is visible in communities that Democrats once treated as reliable territory. Voters who punch clocks, drive trucks, weld steel and keep the lights on are reassessing their affiliations. They want good jobs, affordable housing, manageable household costs and a realistic path to a better life through honest work. Those priorities increasingly align with Republican arguments about growth, production and opportunity rather than with the older Democratic formula of union leadership, expansive government programs and cultural messaging that often feels like socialism and distant from reality.

Union leadership has long been closely tied to the Democratic Party, yet rank-and-file members do not always follow. The 2024 presidential election offered a clear illustration. The Teamsters declined to endorse either Republican Donald Trump or Democrat Kamala Harris after months of internal polling and member interviews. The union cited deep divisions and limited commitments from both candidates. Its polling showed Trump receiving majority support among members in surveys during the campaign. Leadership stayed neutral while many members did not.
news.summary: For generations, the political map of America was simple and stable.

news.title: Democrats are running from Kamala Harris' endorsements
news.text:
Democrats in the toughest midterm races can’t put enough distance between themselves and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

A string of Democratic candidates campaigning in red states have rejected Harris’ support both before and after it was offered. From Alaska to Kansas, Harris’ king-making ability appears nonexistent.

'Having someone from California come in and try to tell Kansans who they should vote for is a pretty bad idea.'

“It’s all good,” Harris spokesman Eduardo Negron told Politico. “Vice President Harris will continue to raise money and travel on behalf of candidates in races where she can help make a difference.”

Harris might not be doing much traveling.

Alaska’s Mary Peltola went out of her way to snub a fundraising assistance offer from Harris in August. 

“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,” a Peltola spokesperson told local outlet KTUU.

The former congresswoman also refused to endorse Harris in 2024, though she clarified in a social media post at the time that she wasn’t voting for President Donald Trump.

RELATED: Is the DSA about to scalp another establishment Democrat?

 Rep. Mary Peltola (D). Ellen Schmidt/Las Vegas Review-Journal/Tribune News Service/Getty Images 

“Mary Peltola stood by as Kamala Harris restricted Alaska’s energy production, including ANWR, and she’d shutter Alaskan energy and jeopardize jobs once again if elected,” National Republican Senate Committee press secretary Bernadette Breslin told Blaze News when asked about Peltola’s move.

Harris isn’t finding takers across the Midwest either. 

“I received 9,000 more votes than Harris in 2024,” Democrat candidate for Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District Rebecca Cooke said in a statement to Politico. “I don’t need anyone to come and campaign with me in my district. I do the work of building relationships — including across the aisle — on my own.”

Though Cooke is distancing herself from Harris now, she was an outspoken supporter during the 2024 presidential election. 

Cooke previously and unsuccessfully ran for the same congressional seat in 2022 and 2024.

Iowa Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek gave a flat “no” when asked if he wanted the former vice president’s help on the campaign trail. Rob Sand, the Democrat running for governor of Iowa, provided Politico a similarly unenthusiastic response.

“Nope,” Sand said. “Let’s move on.” 

Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton, who is also running for the U.S. Senate, shooed the former vice president away from his race a bit more diplomatically.

“Having somebody from California come in and try to tell Kansans who they should vote for is a pretty bad idea,” the Methodist pastor told Politico.

Hamilton’s campaign is widely considered a long shot. Kansas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and he’s lagging several points behind Sen. Roger Marshall (R), even in Democrat-leaning polls.

Though Hamilton may be trying to draw a line between Harris’ West Coast wokeness and his Midwest moderation, his track record suggests there isn’t much daylight between the two. The Methodist pastor admonished his congregation and called on them to scrutinize their white privilege in 2020.

Hamilton’s Resurrection church also touts extensive LGBTQ+ programming, and he has repeatedly landed in hot water for his unorthodox theological views. 

Though she's striking out in the heartland, Harris is finding some purchase with Southern Democrats. 

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, now running for Senate, accepted a Harris endorsement in October 2025 and previously called the former vice president as “my friend Kamala.”

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff is also quietly embracing Harris as he tries to win another term. The pair held a closed-door “Women for Ossoff” tele-rally in August, which was quickly slammed by his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins.

Harris faces uneven terrain looking ahead to a 2028 run. Many in her own party would like her to just go away already, but a few stalwart supporters could make it to the Senate this November.

 Either way, Democrats' tumultuous rebrand isn't over yet.

news.title: Reform is a party in crisis
news.text:
Deputy heads have rolled. Reform UK, in the person of chairman Lee Anderson, announced this morning that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s right hand man, and James Orr, the party’s head of strategy, have stood down and abandoned the party conference. ‘They have left the building and they won’t be coming back,’ Anderson said.

Footage screened by Channel 4 on Thursday night showed Jukes appearing to suggest a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000. A reporter posed as a UK-based son of an American father, who was to give money to the son to give to Reform after being wooed by both Orr and Jukes. Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK. In a statement, Jukes said: ‘I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name.’

“It worked, boom.” That’s Nigel Farage celebrating a Reform UK plot to break election law – by having a US company secretly pay for three influential political polls that benefitted the party.Earlier in the investigation, Reform’s Head of Policy James Orr and senior advisor… pic.twitter.com/jJD7Xn1lLu— Channel 4 News (@Channel4News) September 3, 2026

For a party exposed for apparently operating in a quite different fashion to conventional parties, this was a reassuringly traditional response to crisis, one which has governed British politics for a thousand years – kill the aides in the hope you can save the king.

Anyone who knows anything about Reform, knows what a big deal this is. Orr was one of the figures from the world of think tanks and ideas who gave the party intellectual credibility. Jukes is like a son to Farage, a prickly working class lad from Sutton Coldfield with Essex Boy vibes who has been with Farage for a decade and is effectively his guard dog. Given any choice at all there is no way Farage would ever have thrown him under a bus. That he has gone is a measure of the seriousness of the situation.

Faces at their conference in Birmingham, themed around the first 100 days of a Reform government, are near universally ashen. Spare a thought for the director of communications, Ed Sumner, who spent his 30th birthday fire fighting this mess.

The initial reaction, of course, was to attack the expose as a ‘hoax’ on Reform perpetrated by a bunch of climate change activists. The undercover filming was carried out by Verbatim Investigations, founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. But I’m afraid this is too serious to dismiss with a machine gunning of the messenger, as Reform’s actions this morning tacitly acknowledge.

Farage has just called the sting ‘entrapment’ and insisted his party had ‘done nothing wrong’. But even he admitted the recordings ‘don’t look good, and that’s why we’ve taken the action we have’. They ‘said things that shouldn’t have been said,’ he told LBC. The footage appeared to show both Jukes and Orr explaining to a potential donor how the rules could be circumvented. It was not the other way around.

Farage should also be cognisant that the mood in the bars around Birmingham last night was utterly mutinous. Those who are putting themselves forward as Reform candidates confided their despair. ‘We are giving up our businesses and putting family lives on hold to fight for Reform and this is going on behind the scenes,’ one said.

I caveat what follows with the usual observations. A police investigation seems inevitable, and Reform is carrying out an internal probe. It is necessary to assume that the footage run by Channel 4 was fairly edited and that nothing significantly exculpatory was excluded.

The overwhelming reaction in my WhatsApp groups from operatives in the other main parties was incredulity at the recklessness of it all. ‘If this is how they talk to people they don’t know, imagine what they are saying to people they trust,’ observed one former Downing Street Tory. Channel 4 redacted several of Jukes’ comments but he appeared to be explaining how Reform had previously got donations in what must be assumed to be a similar fashion.

All political parties need more money than they have got, but the art of extracting it is knowing where the rules can be stretched and where they cannot. It is about knowing what is fair game and what sends the shark jumping over the line of propriety. ‘There is no way anyone who has ever worked in CCHQ would talk like that,’ a Conservative staffer said. The view of Labour and Lib Dem operators was much the same. ‘It’s just rank unprofessionalism,’ a Lib Dem said.

So why did they do it? It is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture. The worrying thing for Farage admirers is that if Jukes and Orr behaved like this it is because they believed it to be okay by the boss. Both boasted on camera of their closeness to the leader. In the meeting at the pub with the fake donor, Farage seemed both au fait with how the money would be transferred to Reform, and grateful for it.

The scrappy, sod the rules, bugger the establishment vibe comes from him. This is another reminder of the timeless rule that every major politician’s greatest strength is also their greatest weakness. Farage’s insurgent image has put him in a place where he might win power but made his operation demonstrably less suitable to exercise it.

We needn’t get too pious about this. The last five prime ministers have been, more or less, a failure and Farage might yet earn the right to try his hand. But when you are trying to transform a broken country, anything that sidelines you for a day is a problem. Anderson called the revelations ‘a big distraction’. And you don’t need to be as prim as Miss Jean Brodie to think governments making laws for the rest of us ought to give a passing impression of wanting to stick to them.

I’ve used this line many times, but one of the best Spads I’ve worked with used to tell his ministers: ‘If you don’t want to read about it on the front page of the Daily Mail, don’t do it.’ Inside Reform, the footage suggests that the attitude is that the mainstream media are out to get them, the Electoral Commission are dolts and the rules are for losers.

It remains to be seen whether, as Anderson put it, ‘they’re gone for good’. I can well imagine a world in which Jukes, in particular, is back at Farage’s side in the medium term.

But the wider lesson is that Farage’s view that personal loyalty is the most important attribute, above competence, intelligence, probity or a working knowledge of politics is a potentially dangerous one. It is totally the case that Farage thrives in ecosystems which resemble family rather than a traditional political party. But he’s trying to portray himself as a prime minister in waiting and (even he realises) does not yet have the heavy hitters he needs to ram through landmark changes to the way Britain is governed.

Jukes is a canny character, well plugged into the tropes and tactics of the new right, but he has literally no governing experience and an in-built resentment of the political establishment – one which has often served him well but may now have been his undoing. Very few things raised more eyebrows last night than his claim, downing pints outside the Westminster Arms, that he would become chief of staff in Downing Street, arguably the second most important job in government and one which usually requires a working knowledge of Whitehall. ‘Dan Jukes versus Antonia Romeo [the Cabinet Secretary] is something I want to see,’ said one Tory virtually in near-Earth orbit on schadenfreude. (p.s. it’s a shame no one used the headline: THE HAZARDS OF JUKES this morning)

The other Reform specific observation here is that Farage and his team are just a little too intoxicated by the American right. Farage’s relationship with Donald Trump could yet prove very useful if he becomes prime minister while Trump is in the White House. But his gang have been going to new right conferences for years and are totally immersed in the tactics and issues of MAGA world and the online right. They spent years telling the left ‘Twitter is not real life’ but seem to have succumbed to believing that every approach which works for Trump can also work here. And the infatuation with American money is one always likely to end in tears.

The irony is that Reform’s closeness to the Trumpies ought to have made it easier for them to run due diligence on the prospective ‘donor’. ‘Did they Google this amazingly rich man,’ says the former No. 10 Tory. Another asks: ‘Would they not have asked the GOP [Republicans] if anyone had heard of this guy. You never get a rake thin right wing American donor. I want to see a piggie.’

The pollsters embroiled in this debacle are also in crisis. I have worked with James Johnson on and off since he was Theresa May’s No. 10 numbers man. As I’m sure Johnson would be the first to point out, he has behaved like an utter berk. It’s a pity because he has always seemed to me both humble and serious. JL Partners said in a statement that it is ‘reviewing (its) procedures in order to eliminate possible grey areas and ambiguities and strengthen our safeguards for the future.’

The one point I would make in Johnson’s defence is that JL Partners are good pollsters. They have a commendable record of accuracy and called the last US election right when others were predicting a Kamala Harris win. I have also known pollsters, during a 25-year-career in journalism, who will give both parties and newspapers the answers they want, ask the questions in a certain way or flat out keep asking them until they get what the client requires. That is emphatically not Johnson’s MO.

Indeed, in several regards, Reform did not get what they wanted from the polls featured in the expose. The union workers polling showed that a majority (52 per cent) of union members wanted to affiliate with Labour, not Reform. A majority (51 per cent) of union members said Labour best represents working people, not Reform. It is even the case that Keir Starmer beat Farage on the measure of who would make the best PM with union members, at the nadir of Starmer’s popularity.

It is for the police and Electoral Commission to determine what happens to him and the Reform duo. But it is quite something for the Daily Telegraph to falsely claim they commissioned the poll they ran and then ditch JL Partners when they got caught with their trousers down.

Reform high command hopes that when Farage addresses the conference he will have such big announcements that they will blow all this out of the water. Perhaps. The party – Robert Jenrick, Richard Tice and Zia Yusuf – are offering credible plans for power.

This conference was supposed to show they have the plans to save the country. Their plan for government is taking shape. But, as many observed when Boris Johnson was in No. 10, ‘character is destiny’ and character is what you do in the dark when you think no one is looking. On that front they have more, rather than fewer, questions to answer.

These points are linked. Even those who don’t care about propriety must know that the stench of incompetence is the real killer in politics.

news.title: Trump Wants The Midterms To Be All About Him. Republicans Are Going Along.
news.text:
President Donald Trump wants the midterm elections to be all about Donald Trump. Republicans think they have little choice but to go along.

On Thursday night, a group of more than two dozen Republicans went to the White House Rose Garden to hear Trump address them in the run-up to the midterm elections, now 60 days away. There, after telling the assembled members of Congress how the old Rose Garden would ruin women’s shoes and how he invented the insult “Dumocrat,” Trump claimed he would help them win.

“Whether you’re a good president or a great president, you lose the midterms,” Trump said, acknowledging a historical pattern that has existed since the dawn of the republic. “We’re going to turn that around because there’s no reason for it. … I’ll be at every one of your states, your cities, wherever it is that you’re running.”

The Republicans in attendance included the GOP candidates for governor in Wisconsin, Arizona and Michigan; the party’s Senate candidate in Georgia and members running for reelection in heavily contested House districts in Virginia, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Michigan, Florida, Alaska and Colorado. 

Many of those Republicans ― or at least the political operatives working for them ― are fully aware they don’t really want the president to show up in their districts. Trump is deeply unpopular, with voter anger at his decision to launch a costly war in Iran and his failure to lower prices driving his approval rating down into the 30s in most public opinion surveys. 

But downballot Republicans, who have seen their majorities in the House and Senate become deeply endangered, are not responding by breaking with Trump. They long ago decided on a midterm strategy of tying themselves to the president in hopes of turning out low-propensity conservative voters, and they are desperate for his political operation to spend the hundreds of millions of dollars he has hoarded so far. 

“We need his money and we need his voters,” said one Republican consultant working on a handful of toss-up races around the country, requesting anonymity to speak frankly about his party’s poor standing. “If we can get those things, and convince middle-of-the-road voters Democrats are extremists, that’s how we salvage a good night.”

The consultant acknowledged the plan’s shortcomings, expressing a fear now common among Republicans about Trump keeping most of MAGA, Inc.’s $400 million cash on hand. “Trump is not inherently a generous guy. He could keep all the money.” (Senate Majority Leader John Thune went on Fox News on Tuesday to beg Trump’s super PAC to spend money in Texas, where Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton is trailing Democrat James Talarico in polling.) 

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a moderate Republican who is retiring rather than running for reelection, said Trump is bringing down the GOP’s chances of holding his district, which includes the city of Omaha and its suburbs. Political forecasters expect Democrats to flip the seat in November. 

“Some of the policies and some of the statements aren’t helpful,” Bacon told HuffPost, referring in particular to the president’s tariffs on imported goods, which can put upward pressure on prices. “You get to see it in polling in my district; he’s in the mid-30s, which just makes it hard on Republicans.”

While former Vice President Kamala Harris won Bacon’s district in 2024, Trump is becoming a problem for Republicans across the map. House Majority PAC, which is controlled by allies of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), has found Trump’s approval rating underwater in every district it has recently polled — including a district in South Texas where he won by 18 percentage points in 2024. 

Trump is nonetheless determined to put himself at the center of the midterm conversation. On Thursday, his political operation finally allowed some of its money to dribble out and began airing two ads through a nonprofit group, Keep America Great. 

While one largely echoes the messages Republicans prefer, playing up the elimination of taxes on tips and overtime, the other is simply a paean to the president, featuring footage from Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White’s speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention where he called Trump “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met.” 

“I hope the taxes one airs a lot more than the other,” one Republican media consultant, requesting anonymity to speak frankly about the ads, texted HuffPost, adding sarcastically: “I’m not sure if Dana White is a trusted surrogate for voters.” 

Former Rep. Reid Ribble of Wisconsin, who became one of the first Republicans to criticize Trump when he was running for president in 2015, pointed to the convention, which will take place over two nights in Dallas next week, as emblematic of the symbiosis between Trump and the GOP. 

“They’re going to do that goofy convention down in Texas, and Trump is going to make things about himself because he believes that he’s got all this great power with the voters, while simultaneously ignoring the polling that shows his favorability ratings are in the toilet,” Ribble said. 

Many House Republicans told HuffPost they would attend the convention, describing it as a key part of how the party could convince Trump voters who might otherwise sit out the midterms to show up and stop what they view as a Democratic Party controlled by extremists. 

“It’s important to use every single platform we possibly can to get the message out and show the contrast between the Republican Party and the Democrat[ic] Party,” Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said. 

“I’m assuming — bad thing to do — that the president will make the case that he is actually on the ballot, and it is important for people to come out and vote in 2026,” Rep. Glenn Thompson (R-Pa.) said. 

Other Republicans won’t attend. Rep. Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.) said he’s taking his daughter to visit colleges. Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) said he’ll be in Dallas, but isn’t sure about this schedule. Rep. Kevin Kiley, who changed his affiliation from Republican to independent to protest his party’s approach to a government shutdown last year, seemed baffled by the question. 

“I don’t know much about it. I have no idea,” Kiley said. 

One House lawmaker told HuffPost it was “concerning” that the event’s dates overlap with the first two games of the NFL season.

As much as Republicans may be stuck running on Trump’s record, Democrats have said they don’t actually plan on featuring the president much in advertising, in part due to the former reality television star’s media ubiquity. The exception, they said, would be for Republicans in blue areas like Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Rep. Mike Lawler of New York. 

So are they going to the convention? Collins has said she isn’t. But Lawler dodged the question when HuffPost asked.

“Got to do a lot of things as a candidate,” he said. “You guys spend so much time on inside-baseball nonsense. It’s comical.”

The New York Times reported on Thursday that Lawler would attend, introducing a constituent whose daughter was killed by an undocumented immigrant.

news.title: Red State Dems to Kamala: Lady, Stay the Hell Away From Me
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is revving up her involvement in the midterms. While some Democrats are eager to embrace her, others want her to steer clear.

Harris had kept a relatively low profile so far on the campaign trail. Some Democrats prefer it that way.

Iowa’s two most prominent Democratic candidates have said they do not want Harris to campaign for them. Alaska’s Democratic Senate nominee rejected a fundraising solicitation Harris sent on her behalf. And a swing-district Democrat in Wisconsin and a long-shot Senate hopeful in Kansas both told POLITICO they would prefer Harris keep her distance.

“I received 9,000 more votes than Harris in 2024,” Rebecca Cooke, the Democratic challenger to Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden in western Wisconsin, said in a statement when asked by POLITICO. “I don’t need anyone to come and campaign with me in my district. I do the work of building relationships — including across the aisle — on my own.”

“In Kansas, you’re trying to reach 45 percent of the state who are Republicans and a lot of really good people who are Republicans, but their vantage point or their worldview may be a bit different than Kamala Harris’,” Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton told POLITICO. “What I’m looking at is I’m really mounting a very Kansas-centered campaign, and I’m out speaking, I tell people I’m running as an independent-minded Democrat.”

Hamilton is running an uphill battle in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. The state is seen as potentially somewhat in play amid the ongoing war in Iran, trade wars with close allies and a persistent cost of living crisis that have cut especially deep in agricultural territory.

But that doesn’t mean a coastal Democrat like Harris would play well in the conservative heartland.

“Having somebody from California come in and try to tell Kansans who they should vote for is a pretty bad idea,” Hamilton said. Harris has not endorsed in the race.

news.title: New HBO superhero show faces 'woke' criticism for reframing classic hero lore around racial privilege
news.text: HBO’s new superhero series, "Lanterns," drew criticism from some viewers who accused the studio of overhauling a beloved character’s origin story to focus on modern racial discourse and privilege. Episode 3, "OutKast," reframes the franchise's traditional emphasis on "fearlessness" through the experience of a Black man in America, prompting some critics to accuse the show of sacrificing classic comic book lore for social justice commentary. In DC Comics lore, Green Lanterns are intergalactic peacekeepers chosen by alien power rings that seek out individuals with the innate ability to overcome fear. In "Lanterns," that standard is reframed as an unfair burden when applied to Stewart. BELOVED 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' FACES WAGONLOAD OF 'WOKE' ALLEGATIONS OVER NETFLIX REBOOT "Do you know the differences in race on Earth?" Stewart's mother, Bernadette, asks an alien Guardian of the Universe who has taken the form of an older White woman. "Do you understand how unfair it is to ask a Black man in America if he’s afraid? "We are terrified daily of persecution and still show up, sometimes better than everyone around us," Bernadette adds. "Even in space, y’all don’t consider us." Rather than being chosen as an adult for his ability to overcome fear, Stewart is conditioned by his parents from infancy in "Lanterns" to wield the ring through hyper-precise perfection. Some viewers accused the show of replacing the hero’s traditional emphasis on individual willpower with a lesson on racial privilege. "Lanterns" co-creator Damon Lindelof also created HBO’s 2019 superhero series "Watchmen," which similarly drew criticism over its focus on American racial politics. But not everyone online objected to the changes. 'THE BOYS' CREATOR ADMITS 'SINKING FEELING' AS REALITY 'OUT-CRAZIES' HIS POLITICAL FINAL SEASON "Lanterns is fantastic. And for those inevitably crying that they ruined GL by going ‘woke,’ you obviously never read O’Neil & Adams’ Green Lantern/Green Arrow run," filmmaker and comic book writer Steven DeKnight, who previously worked on "Daredevil," wrote on X. The character John Stewart debuted in 1971 as one of DC’s first Black superheroes. He was portrayed as a civil rights advocate who challenged authorities in Detroit and as a fearless leader whose willpower earned him the Green Lantern ring. Critics argue that "Lanterns" alters that characterization by making Stewart’s childhood conditioning, rather than his natural willpower, central to his selection. "Lanterns" writer and co-executive producer Vanessa Baden Kelly addressed the character’s comic origins and accusations that the show had gone "woke" in an interview with TheWrap. ISSA RAE SAYS DEI HAS BECOME A 'BAD WORD' IN HOLLYWOOD AS EXECUTIVES OF COLOR 'TIPTOE' TO KEEP JOBS "I stumbled across some people calling the show ‘woke,’ and there were people putting panels in the reactions and the comments, and they were panels from the 1970s John Stewart," Baden Kelly said. "Him calling people ‘Whitey’ or him opposing wars, and I’m like, ‘Oh my God.’ I read a bunch, but I couldn’t read all of it, and you’re just like, that’s right, just keep it in the front of your mind — that this is who John Stewart’s always been," she added. In the same article, J. Alphonse Nicholson, who plays the hero's father, John Stewart Sr., in flashbacks, discussed the show’s portrayal of racial dynamics. "I’m just grateful that the writing room put this into the script," Nicholson told TheWrap. "How can you expect this African American man in this world … to be fearless? It really raises a lot of questions on who has the privilege to move through life without thinking about those things, even in the fictional world." Nicholson also linked the show to the 2024 presidential election during an appearance on pop culture creator Fantastic Frankey’s podcast, arguing the country is experiencing the consequences of "not trusting a Black woman." "Could you imagine where we would be right now if Kamala got up in there, dog? Could you imagine how we would’ve been? It’d be a lot different, right? So we’re experiencing the consequences of not trusting a Black woman," Nicholson said in the clip, connecting the show’s themes of heroism to Harris’ 2024 candidacy. KELSEY GRAMMER ADMITS IT'S 'EXHAUSTING' WHEN MOVIES TRY TO ALTER HISTORY TO FIT MODERN TASTES "And now we have this show in a way that can [kind of] tell you how great it could be. How great of a superhero we can create and have if you trust a Black woman." Entertainment critic Christian Toto argued the creative choices in "Lanterns" reflect a broader trend in modern-day entertainment. "Today's Hollywood screenwriters care little about canon or fidelity to the source material," Christian Toto, host of "The Hollywood in Toto Podcast," told Fox News Digital. "They love injecting modern culture war battles into storylines, even when they don't mesh with the material or present themselves as awkward and unnecessary." Toto argued that the show’s dialogue risks alienating audiences despite what he described as "strong ratings." "That's precisely what's happening with the show so far. Make no mistake. This is overtly woke in nature. The scribes are jamming social justice arguments into the dialogue in ways that feel inauthentic to the time period in question. Even worse? The on-the-nose dialogue takes us out of the story," Toto said. "The pushback was inevitable. Audiences sense this kind of clunky woke storytelling a mile away. And many are exhausted by it. Yet the series is getting strong ratings to date, so general audiences are so interested in the comic book characters they'll often look past the woke detours. At least for now." She was hit with a single count of wire fraud earlier this week and faces up to 20 years behind bars if convicted. Steel has yet to enter a plea but remains on bail. 

On Wednesday, she took to LinkedIn and wrote an all-capital letters post saying: 'Believe none of what you hear and a small fraction of what you see!!' 

The complaint against Steel, seen by the Daily Mail, claimed she used a phony letter from Deutsche Bank to claim that she held an account with around $350 million in it to swindle money from a California-based entrepreneur.

Investigators at Deutsche probed the letter and later told investigators that it was a fake, the complaint said.

Prosecutors allege in the criminal complaint that it was part of a scheme by Steel to present herself as being credible.

The complaint also painted Steel as being a serial fabricator who used her social media and YouTube to falsely give the impression of being a successful businesswoman. 

Such lies, the complaint claimed, saw her managing to be given a Lifetime President Achievement Award by President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris. 

That award was set up to honor Americans who dedicated over 4,000 hours of volunteering. Steel is said to have lied about completing those volunteer hours to further enhance her image. 

Records seen by the Daily Mail indicate that Steel has a history of bankruptcy and unemployment. 

In 2014 she filed for bankruptcy saying that she was unemployed, had a small amount of money in her checking account and was due over $18,800 to creditors.

She also currently lives at home with her mother in a comfortable but modest $500,000 home in a quiet suburb, that sits close to a McDonald's, according to public records.

And while Steel's own website painted her as an Ambassador to the Central African Republic, federal prosecutors said she was never a diplomat. 

Images posted on her site include images of her with former Namibian President Hage Geingob, it is unclear when these pictures were taken.

The complaint highlighted a series of posts to her Facebook and Instagram page, which have since been deleted, in which she addressed herself as Ambassador Steel.

Quoting her posts, the complaint said she had posted Instagram saying: 'I was just sworn in as Ambassador for Central African Republic to the United States.'

A post to her Facebook page continued the charade, the complaint claimed, saying she posted: 'I put a whole country on my back #AMBASSADOR STEEL.'

Despite her claims, the complaint said: 'Records with the US Department of State's Office of Foreign Missions indicate that [Steel] is not an accredited diplomat. 

'Nor is she an employee of the United States Government in any capacity as an Ambassador or diplomat to any other country.'

In reference to the presidential award, the complaint said that an associate of hers, identified only as 'LG', put her forward for the award after Steel asked them to. 

'LG' has since spoken with federal investigators, claiming that she signed off on the volunteering hours after just looking at Steel's resume, the complaint added.

'Steel's award was inconsistent with program guidelines and requirements and would not have been genuinely awarded given the information provided', the complaint said.

The complaint also alleged that Steel made public comments that she had acquired an Embassy Suites by Hilton. 

Those comments, which are still live on US Times Now, also saw her claim she carried out a renovation at the property worth $3 million and turned it into a Wyndham Hotel. 

Federal investigators claimed in their complaint that they spoke with officials in Southfield, where the hotel was said to be, who told them they never issued a Certificate of Occupancy meaning it was never authorized to open. 

A separate federal case filed against her by the owners of Wyndham, Ramada Worldwide, saw the company awarded $1.5 million after she breached their franchise agreement, a federal judge in New Jersey found.

Her website and social media pages also pointed to her owning 'Steel Private Bank', but the complaint said that such a company was never registered with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).

It added: 'Based on the aforementioned facts, Shannon Steel has displayed a public persona as the owner of a bank with significant assets, an Ambassador, and a successful hotel owner, with representations that are either materially false or grossly misleading. 

'During the course of investigation into conduct of Shannon Steel between 2022 and present, investigators with the FBI, IRS, and DSS spoke with investors and business partners of Steel who referenced their knowledge and research of these achievements as reasons, at least in part, of why they found her a credible and trustworthy individual with whom to invest.'

Deutsche told investigators that the letter Steel is alleged to have used was 'not issued by us and is not authentic.' 

Steel was released on a $10,000 unsecured bond following a hearing in federal court earlier this week, court records said. 

The Daily Mail contacted Steel and her attorney for comment.
news.summary: Shannon Monet Steel, 42, told people she kept her nine-figure fortune in her own private bank and that she was an Ambassador to the Central African Republic.

news.title: Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton, Oprah Winfrey and others pay tribute to Gloria Steinem
news.text:
Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure.

The celebrated author and activist, who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the U.S. women’s movement, died Wednesday at her home in New York City. She was 92.

 Kamala Harris 

“To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders, and her advocacy was always about fighting for the strength, intelligenc, and dignity of women everywhere. She showed incredible support for women running for office, and I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency.” — the former vice president, on Facebook.

 Hillary Clinton 

“Gloria Steinem was, at heart, an optimist. Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice she made every day. Even though we’ve faced setbacks to women’s full participation and equality in America and around the world, I want Gloria’s voice to remain in our heads.” — the former secretary of state, on social media.

 Oprah Winfrey 

“Every woman who has ever walked into a room knowing she belongs there; every woman who has demanded equal pay, equal respect, ownership of her own body, and the right to make her own choices; every girl who has grown up assuming that her dreams are hers to pursue — whether she knows Gloria Steinem’s name or not — is living, in some measure, inside the progress Gloria helped create.” — the media mogul and television producer, on social media.

 Nancy Pelosi 

“May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.” — former Speaker of the House, on X.

 Jane Fonda 

“For decades, she trudged through every airport in the country, in sandals and a trench, carrying her own suitcase, packed with a few black clothes, hair curlers, and steam iron, in order to speak to women — at conferences, town halls, consciousness raising groups. No group was too small to deserve Gloria’s time. This is how she built the new women’s movement.” — actor and activist, on Instagram.

 Barbra Streisand 

“From the first moment I met Gloria in the 1970s, I was deeply impressed by her. She stood for everything I believed in: equality for women in the workplace, a woman’s right to choose, greater political representation for women, and a thoughtful, determined response to every form of gender-based discrimination. She gave voice to these issues with fierce intelligence and steely determination, but also with wit, empathy, and humility. What made her so extraordinary was not only the strength of her convictions, but the humanity and grace with which she expressed them.” — singer and actor, on social media.

 Jill Biden 

“Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls. She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward.” — the former first lady, on social media.

 Melinda French Gates 

“Generational change doesn’t happen by accident or fate — it takes leaders like Gloria Steinem who work hand in hand with so many others to build a lasting movement.. What a light she was for me and so many others. What a debt we owe her.” — the philanthropist and businesswoman, on social media.

 Julie Taymor 

“She got tremendous joy out of being with other people, with other women, and improving their lives. ... She understood about working from the bottom up — and she never really wanted credit for any of it. She always said if she wasn’t alive, there would still be a women’s movement. I think she underestimated her power. She was very modest. She had not an ounce of, you know, narcissism or ‘me, me, me’ about her. And she was able to really make change.” — the director of “The Glorias,” a 2020 biopic of Steinem, in an interview with The Associated Press.

 Julianne Moore 

“The time I spent studying Gloria Steinem in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life. Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave.” — the actor, who played Steinem in the 2020 film “The Glorias,” on Instagram.

 Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex 

“Privately, she was even better than you would imagine — spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit.” — Duchess of Sussex, on Instagram.

 Roxane Gay 

“Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy.” — the writer, on Instagram.

 Abigail Disney 

“Everything Gloria did was rooted in kindness. It flowed through her political activism.” — her friend and fellow activist, to the AP.

 Rachel Cargle 

“Gloria, you changed my life. You seeded a fire in me that would result in my own activism. I am forever grateful to have learned from what you offered the world.” — the author and social justice activist, commenting on Instagram.

 Harvey Fierstein 

“An unstoppable visionary who demanded an equal role for females in a male dominated world and worked tirelessly, for decades, to bring that change about. The greatest irony was how many women she had to battle as they cowered behind their male owners. But battle she did. Equal rights! Freedom to choose! Access to political power! Equal pay for equal effort.” — the actor and playwright, on social media. 

 Jill Filipovic 

“I have done what I wanted to do with my life. That would not have been possible without Steinem and the scores of other feminists who it is no exaggeration to say radically reshaped America and the world.” — the author and feminist, in her Substack newsletter.
news.summary: Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure

news.text:
House Speaker Mike Johnson already knows what the Republican-dominated Supreme Court is in for when Democrats get big-enough control of Congress and the White House, writes Slate’s Alexis Romero. That’s why Johnson tried to pass a new law out of the House to stop it.

“Johnson … led an effort Wednesday to amend the Constitution and cap the number of Supreme Court justices at nine. Since the size of the court is currently set by federal law, not by the Constitution, Johnson said the amendment was necessary to stop Democrats from adding justices to the court,” wrote Romero. “Over the course of 24 hours, Johnson announced his plan to introduce the amendment and had it brought to the House floor, only for it to immediately fail along party lines.”

President Donald Trump has been having a bit of a romp lately with his tailor-made Republican Supreme Court imparting huge new power to the executive and legal immunity for Trump to do as he wills with state agencies, immigration and the very face of Washington DC., and the White House. Romero said “it doesn’t take a brain surgeon (or even a lawyer) to understand why the leader of the House GOP would like to keep in place a Supreme Court with six Republican appointees,” but he added that these kinds of legislative efforts are extremely rare coming from any speaker.

But New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie pointed out that “Democrats are getting serious about court reform.” Former Vice President and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris also officially advocated for expanding the court from nine to 13 justices because the country already has 13 intermediate courts of appeal and a 13-member Supreme Court would allow each justice to review motions from a lower court one-to-one.

But Johnson wants Congressional Republicans to jettison the power to expand the court before Democrats use it to neutralize the conservative majority that granted Trump immunity from crimes while in the White House and nearly removed Constitutional birthright citizenship.

Romero called it an extreme bid by the Speaker for “constitutional self-castration.”

“But Republican legislators would rather sabotage their own chamber’s constitutional authority than allow Democrats the chance to reform the court,” said Romero. “In opposition to Johnson’s proposal, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark noted that the amendment would strip Congress of ‘yet another constitutional authority that is meant to be controlled by the American people’s representatives.’”

“Think for a second about the moral calculus the GOP is doing,” urged Romero. “We’re talking about a system of congressional authority over the court that has lasted for 250 years. And Republicans are so scared of the electorate voting for judicial reform that they would eliminate a key piece of that century-old authority in the two months before they’re likely voted out of office.”

But the court-reform debate is raging, said Romero, because the nation’s high court is deeply detached from the public. It is a court that “avoids contending with ethics complaints against its own members, while blessing ethical violations in the White House.” Its judges demand the privacy of no cameras in its chambers, while allowing states to “invade the private medical decisions of women across the country,” he said. It’s also a court that “anonymously votes behind closed doors in secret rulings, and does so in support of Trump’s not-so-secret effort to disenfranchise votes by mail.”

“Until all of that changes, court reform will be top of mind and top of discussion, no matter what the Republicans try to do before November,” Romero assured.

news.title: Stop the Democrats’ scheme to pack the Supreme Court
news.text:
Democrats are in a quandary over the Supreme Court. Every four years, they’ve warned their voters that electing a Republican president will lead to more conservative Supreme Court justices. And yet since Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980 through today, they’ve lost more presidential elections than they’ve won. Maybe the voters are telling Democrats something. Maybe Americans don’t want the court packed with Sonia Sotomayors who make up or rewrite the laws as they see fit.

So now the left is angry over the tilt of the court, which has six conservatives and three liberals.

Why? Because elections have consequences. Sorry, this is the price you pay for nominating Michael Dukakis, John Kerry, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. They aren’t exactly hanging around anywhere near the 50-yard line on political ideology.

Now we have Democrats divided on what to do next. Many want Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Elizabeth Warren to be their next presidential nominee. There’s no learning curve here.

In the meantime, while Donald Trump is still president, they want urgent action. On the one hand, the democratic socialists want to abolish the highest court of the land. What they want to replace it with is anyone’s guess.

Other party leaders want to pack the court with four new liberal justices. Franklin Roosevelt tried this court-packing scheme in 1937, and voters rebelled.

But here they go again. On Sunday, Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., raised this possibility and disgracefully played the race card when asked about the Supreme Court’s recent decisions. He accused Republicans of taking “this country back … to those rulings of Justice Taney that said, ‘No black man has any right that a white man must respect.'” He was referring to Supreme Court Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the infamous 1857 Dred Scott opinion just before the Civil War.

Does he even know that for 100 years after the Civil War, Democrats were the party of segregation?

What’s deeply troubling about this war on the Supreme Court is that this is the institution that is the final check against runaway mob-rule democracy that can trample the rights of the minority. That minority could be blacks, Hispanics, gays, immigrants or disabled people. They don’t seem to understand that pure majority-rule democracy is, as the old saying goes, two wolves and a sheep voting on what to have for dinner.

Pure democracy only goes your way until you no longer have 50% plus one voters on your side. Clyburn is right that there have been occasions, like the one from 1857 that he mentioned, when the court has made egregiously wrong decisions. But mostly, the court gets it right. It’s not clear how stacking the court – on the left or the right – could make for more just decisions.

This is why Republicans are so wrong to try to abolish the filibusters in the Senate. We always want to make it HARDER, not easier, to pass new edicts that impair our freedoms.

I, personally, would have no problem expanding the Supreme Court to 12 justices if it could be done in a fair, nonpartisan way. I also strongly support a mandatory retirement age of 75 for all future justices on the court.

But to overly politicize – or, worse, do away with – the Supreme Court and allow Congress to have the last word on the constitutionality of new laws is a dangerous proposition. James Madison once famously described the judiciary as a “bulwark” of our liberties. Hopefully, we will never give up this most important check and balance on runaway government power.
news.summary: 'Maybe Americans don't want the court packed with Sonia Sotomayors who make up or rewrite the laws'

news.title: Kamala Harris Faces Fact Democrats Are Telling Her 'No Thanks'
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris was forced to face reports about other Democrats rebuffing her campaign help this midterm cycle.

While paying tribute to feminist activist Gloria Steinem Thursday on MS NOW, “State of Play” host Peter Alexander asked the 2024 presidential candidate about a Politico story citing a range of Democratic candidates in red states and rural areas who want her to stay away from their races or have flat-out rejected her endorsement offers.

Harris responded, “Listen, Peter, we need to win, OK? Bottom line, we need to win. I have run locally, I’ve run for statewide office, and obviously nationally.”

Though she made sure to highlight her campaign credentials, the California-bred politician said she’ll defer to the candidates who “know what they need to do to win, and I would expect nothing less.”

Either way, Harris said, electing Democrats who will curb President Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s power is her main goal.

She told Alexander, “I look forward to being on the trail and helping folks where I can be helpful, but we have got to put a check on this lawless administration and deliver what Americans need and deserve: lower costs, affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, you name it. So I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win.”

Sources both on and off the record in the Politico piece said they wanted to focus on local politics and weren’t interested in any assists from national-level Democrats.

Senate nominee Adam Hamilton, a Kansas Democrat, put things frankly for Politico, saying, “Having somebody from California come in and try to tell Kansans who they should vote for is a pretty bad idea.”
