news.title: Ryan Reynolds says the 1980s were a traumatic and 'brutal time' — and people aren't happy about it
news.text:
Ryan Reynolds may have a point, but no one is hearing it.

Reynolds was talking about an upcoming film that focuses heavily on American culture in the 1980s when he described what he thinks the decade was really about.

'Sociopolitical tensions everywhere.'

Speaking to a reporter from the red carpet, Reynolds said that looking back at the 1980s now, the decade tends to be seen through rose-colored glasses and not for how it actually was.

"What's interesting about when you get far enough away from a time period that's quite distinct, I think there's always a lovely feeling associated with it. It's almost like you pave over all the trauma with, like, puppy dogs and ice cream," the actor began. "The '80s was a brutal, brutal time for people. It was a f**king mess."

Reynolds was born in Vancouver, Canada, in 1976 and grew up in the province. Now 49, he described the American 1980s as being filled with political tensions.

"It was a tremendous strife," he told Variety. "Sociopolitical tensions everywhere. We were still pretty fresh off a Cuban missile crisis, which was only like 15-20 years before. It’s a tumultuous period, but you look back at it now and you’re like, 'Oh, yeah. "Top Gun." Cocaine!' Like, no! It was really scary."

RELATED: Mark Ruffalo writes endless progressive letters — gets called racist anyways

 Manhattan, 1984. Barbara Alper/Getty Images

Gag him with a spoon

A significant number of notable accounts disagreed with the younger actor's take, with women's sports advocate Jennifer Sey commenting, "Literally no one was talking or worrying about the Cuban Missile Crisis. What is he talking about?!"

"I was born in 1972 and grew up in the 80s. I have no idea what he’s talking about. The 80s were awesome," novelist Mathew Betley wrote on X.

Author Sarah Adams added, "The 80s were amazing, what the hell is this revisionist history."

At least one reader agreed with Reynolds, though, pointing to '80s issues like peer pressure and divorce.

"It was everyone for themselves," he wrote. "Teflon Reagan shining through the sooty shadow of Vietnam and overthrowing democracies in Central America. Quadrupled national debt. Even as a teen I knew it was a bulls**t decade."

RELATED: HBO star declares USA is suffering without Kamala Harris: 'Consequences of not trusting a black woman'

Right said 'Dead'

While the majority of comments strongly disagreed with Reynolds, perhaps the latter reaction was closer to what the "Deadpool" star was referring to.

Reynolds reportedly said that modern popular projects like "Stranger Things" paint a different picture of how society was. Particularly, he said the threat of nuclear war between the U.S. and Soviet Union was surging and the exodus of American manufacturing was devastating the working class. 

This, along with AIDS, serves as the true reality of the time, Reynolds explained.

"I think when you look back at 2026 and this era, I think they're going to pick on the big-ticket items that don't really leave the footprint culturally that you would think it would. I don't know. ... I wonder what it's going to be. Is going to be like, 'Oh, the COVID era' or something. I have no idea," Reynolds concluded.

news.title: Chuck Schumer Dealt Warning Sign About AOC Challenge in New Poll
news.text: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer received another warning sign about his popularity relative to Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez among New York voters, as the progressive congresswoman has been floated as a potential challenger ahead of his 2028 reelection. Ocasio-Cortez, who represents parts of Queens and the Bronx in the House of Representatives, is seen as a new leader of the progressive movement, which gained significant ground in New York during this year’s Democratic primaries. Her next steps will be closely watched over the coming months, as some Democrats expect she will either run for president or challenge Schumer for his Senate seat. Some progressives view her as the best choice for the left in the 2028 presidential race, as it’s not clear who else could occupy the left-leaning lane in the Democratic primary; but others believe she should run for Senate against Schumer, whose popularity has waned as Democratic voters are frustrated with what they view as a lethargic approach to President Donald Trump’s administration. AOC More Popular Than Schumer in New York, Poll Finds A new poll released Thursday by the organization Education Reform Now Advocacy (ERNA) found that Schumer’s popularity in New York lags behind Ocasio-Cortez ahead of a potential 2028 challenge. Schumer’s net favorability rating stood at -13 points, while Ocasio-Cortez’s was +8 points across the state, according to the poll. Fifty-two percent of respondents said they view Schumer unfavorably, compared to 39 percent viewing him favorably and 10 percent who didn’t know. Meanwhile, 47 percent of respondents said they viewed Ocasio-Cortez favorably, with 39 percent viewing her unfavorably and 14 percent unsure, according to the poll. It surveyed 505 respondents in New York from August 19 to 21, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Schumer Has Faced Democratic Backlash Schumer, once a popular figure in the state, has seen diminishing favorability ratings in the second Trump era. He is up for reelection in 2028 and has faced a wave of Democratic backlash over his leadership. Many Democrats have pushed for a more aggressive approach to the Trump administration, though leadership has noted that the party does not control either chamber of Congress and cannot push back on his priorities. Frustration came to a head last year after Schumer helped advance a Republican-backed government funding bill with little fight, yielding no concessions from Republicans. The backlash prompted calls for him to face a primary challenge next year. AOC Favored in Poll, Prediction Markets Over Schumer Ocasio-Cortez has not said whether she plans to run for the Senate, but a poll released last year suggests she would start the primary in a strong position. The poll, conducted by Data for Progress among 767 likely New York Democratic primary voters from March 26 to 31, 2025, showed Ocasio-Cortez with nearly a 20-point lead in a hypothetical 2028 primary matchup between the two. The margin of error associated with the sample size is plus or minus 4 percentage points. Fifty-five percent of respondents said they would pick her over Schumer, while 36 percent said they would stick with the incumbent. An additional 9 percent said they aren't sure who they would vote for. Ocasio-Cortez also leads Schumer on the Kalshi prediction market—she had a 46 percent chance of winning the Senate nomination against Schumer’s 34 percent chance as of Thursday. On Polymarket, however, traders believed she would run for president, not Senate, giving her a 62 percent chance of seeking the presidential nomination. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment in the moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Progressive Surge in New York In 2028, the left will work to capitalize on its momentum from the 2026 midterms to expand its power in New York, which has become the heart of the progressive movement over the past few years. Ocasio-Cortez's 2018 victory began a shift in the state, and progressives have made further inroads since. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have become major power players in state politics, with their candidates winning numerous primaries for state office in 2026. At the federal level, three progressives—Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Brad Lander, and Claire Valdez—won congressional primaries in New York City. Avila-Chevalier and Lander did so by defeating more moderate incumbents. Avila-Chevalier and Valdez are both members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). DSA also scored a major win with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory in the 2025 mayoral race. Mamdani has become another leading face of democratic socialism in the nation's largest city. Could AOC Run for President? Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out running for president. Many on the left view her as the natural heir to Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who occupied the progressive lane in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections. Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, who served as an adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." On Thursday, Politico reported that Mamdani, a democratic socialist and close ally of Ocasio-Cortez, signed a petition from the DSA describing her as “the most viable left contender for president in 2028,” though he has not publicly endorsed her. Typically, candidates begin announcing presidential campaigns after the midterms, so it’s possible some contenders could begin announcing later this year or early in 2027. Some progressives view the Senate race as a safer option for Ocasio-Cortez, particularly given the rise of the left in the Empire State. Not all Democrats are sold on Ocasio-Cortez as a presidential candidate, as many believe a more centrist candidate without DSA affiliations could stand a better chance at winning over moderate and independent voters against a Republican candidate. AOC’s Chances in Democratic Primary: What Polls Show Polls suggest Ocasio-Cortez would be a handful of leading contenders alongside prominent Democrats like former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro. Here's what two recent polls show about Ocasio-Cortez’s chances of winning in 2028 if she runs for president: HarrisX (August 28-30, 2,100 registered voters, MOE +/- 2.1 points) Quantus Insights (August 26-28, 515 likely voters, MOE +/- 3.2 points) What Happens Next Ocasio-Cortez will be closely watched as a potential candidate for both the Senate and presidential races. The primaries are still more than a year away, so she has plenty of time to make her decision before any formal filing deadlines. However, other candidates could begin announcing presidential runs in the coming months, which could create political pressure not to wait too long to enter the race or risk losing early momentum.
